hints.title: Find the first allowed common term
hints.body: List initial terms of each arithmetic sequence until you find a common value. Check that it is the first common value within the actual starting ranges of both sequences.
hints.recap: A remainder condition alone does not encode where a sequence begins.
hints.pitfall: A value before a sequence’s first term is not a member of that sequence.
hints.pause: Find and justify the first allowed common term.

recall.reminder: Identify the actual first term and valid range of an arithmetic block before counting positions.

hints.title: Justify the repeated spacing
hints.body: The difference between two common terms must be a multiple of each original common difference. Find the smallest positive such spacing, then verify that adding it preserves membership in both sequences.
hints.recap: A common spacing requires both divisibility conditions.
hints.pitfall: Seeing two common terms is not by itself a proof of all later ones.
hints.pause: Derive the spacing and justify that no common term lies between consecutive values.

recall.reminder: Read initial terms, then justify the rule that repeats the pattern before using it at a distant position.

hints.title: Use the AP index and divide
hints.body: Write the twentieth common term from the first common term and spacing, remembering the first term uses zero increments. Then reduce the result modulo seven.
hints.recap: The term index determines the number of increments.
hints.pitfall: Twenty increments would give the twenty-first term.
hints.pause: Compute the term or work with remainders to obtain the requested remainder.

recall.reminder: The term index determines the number of increments.

solution:
The first common term is 17. Every difference between two common terms is divisible by 3 and by 5, hence by 15. Conversely, adding 15 preserves membership of both sequences, because 15=5·3=3·5. Thus the common terms are exactly 17,32,47,….

The twentieth common term is N=17+(20−1)·15=17+285=302. Since 302=7·43+1, the remainder is 1: B.

The starting boundary matters: 2 satisfies the same remainder conditions but is not a term of Sequence 1, which begins at 11.
knowledgePattern: Intersect two APs then take a modular remainder
